<cell id="7c374a11"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># Department Co-orders with Produce

The merchandising analytics team wants to understand how frequently different departments are purchased together with Produce.</cell id="7c374a11">
<cell id="68f6f338"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Load and prepare the data

Load the prior purchase history and map each purchased product to its department.</cell id="68f6f338">
<cell id="619d2766">import pandas as pd


DATA_DIR = "../../data/shop"

order_products = pd.read_csv(
    f"{DATA_DIR}/order_products__prior.csv",
    usecols=["order_id", "product_id"],
)

products = pd.read_csv(
    f"{DATA_DIR}/products.csv",
    usecols=["product_id", "department_id"],
)

departments = pd.read_csv(
    f"{DATA_DIR}/departments.csv",
)

order_products = order_products.merge(
    products,
    on="product_id",
    how="left",
)

order_products.head()</cell id="619d2766">

   order_id  product_id  department_id
0         2       33120             16
1         2       28985              4
2         2        9327             13
3         2       45918             13
4         2       30035             13
<cell id="33e09484"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Identify Produce orders

Identify all orders containing at least one Produce product. These orders define the purchase history used for the co-order comparison.</cell id="33e09484">
<cell id="df967eae">produce_id = departments.loc[
    departments["department"].eq("produce"),
    "department_id",
].iloc[0]

produce_orders = order_products.loc[
    order_products["department_id"].eq(produce_id),
    "order_id",
].unique()

print(
    "Produce orders:",
    f"{len(produce_orders):,}",
)</cell id="df967eae">

Produce orders: 2,409,320

<cell id="da6ae01a"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Calculate department co-order counts

Within Produce orders, count purchases from the other departments and rank them by co-order frequency.</cell id="da6ae01a">
<cell id="c1145007">produce_items = order_products[
    order_products["order_id"].isin(produce_orders)
    & order_products["department_id"].ne(produce_id)
]

coorder_counts = (
    produce_items["department_id"]
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("department_id")
    .reset_index(name="coorder_counts")
    .merge(
        departments,
        on="department_id",
        how="left",
    )
    [["department", "coorder_counts"]]
)

print(
    "Purchase records in Produce orders:",
    f"{len(produce_items):,}",
)

print(
    "Departments compared:",
    len(coorder_counts),
)</cell id="c1145007">

Purchase records in Produce orders: 18,679,274
Departments compared: 20

<cell id="ae1843f0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Rank departments

Report the departments with the highest co-order counts in Produce orders.</cell id="ae1843f0">
<cell id="473168d4">print("Top departments purchased with Produce:")

print(
    coorder_counts
    .head(15)
    .to_string(index=False)
)</cell id="473168d4">

dry goods pasta          757995

<cell id="d2a449b0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Visualize department co-orders

Compare the leading departments by co-order count. The chart also reports the number of Produce orders and purchase records represented in the analysis.</cell id="d2a449b0">
<cell id="7b5edf29">import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

top_departments = (
    coorder_counts
    .head(15)
    .sort_values(
        "coorder_counts",
        ascending=True,
    )
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(
    figsize=(10, 6)
)

ax.barh(
    top_departments["department"],
    top_departments["coorder_counts"],
)

ax.set_title(
    "Departments Purchased Most Frequently "
    "in Produce Orders"
)

ax.set_xlabel(
    "Co-order Count"
)

ax.set_ylabel(
    "Department"
)

ax.text(
    0.98,
    0.02,
    (
        f"Produce orders: {len(produce_orders):,}\n"
        f"Top department count: "
        f"{coorder_counts['coorder_counts'].max():,}"
    ),
    transform=ax.transAxes,
    ha="right",
    va="bottom",
    fontsize=9,
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()</cell id="7b5edf29">

The merchandising analytics team wants to understand how frequently different departments are purchased together with Produce.

## Load and prepare the data

Load the prior purchase history and map each purchased product to its department.

import pandas as pd


DATA_DIR = "../../data/shop"

order_products = pd.read_csv(
    f"{DATA_DIR}/order_products__prior.csv",
    usecols=["order_id", "product_id"],

    usecols=["product_id", "department_id"],

    f"{DATA_DIR}/departments.csv",
)

order_products = order_products.merge(
    products,
    on="product_id",
    how="left",
)

order_products.head()

Identify all orders containing at least one Produce product. These orders define the purchase history used for the co-order comparison.

    f"{len(produce_orders):,}",
)

    & order_products["department_id"].ne(produce_id)

    produce_items["department_id"]
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("department_id")
    .reset_index(name="coorder_counts")
    .merge(
        departments,

print(

content.text:
This is the Instacart "shop" dataset (`../../data/shop`), made of 6 CSV files that join on `product_id`, `order_id`, and `department_id`/`aisle_id`:

| File | Columns | Rows (approx) |
|---|---|---|
| `orders.csv` | `order_id, user_id, eval_set, order_number, order_dow, order_hour_of_day, days_since_prior_order` | ~3.4M |
| `order_products__prior.csv` | `order_id, product_id, add_to_cart_order, reordered` | ~32M |
| `order_products__train.csv` | same as above | ~1.4M |
| `products.csv` | `product_id, product_name, aisle_id, department_id` | ~50K |
| `aisles.csv` | `aisle_id, aisle` | 134 |
| `departments.csv` | `department_id, department` | 21 |

Sample rows:

```
=== orders.csv ===
order_id,user_id,eval_set,order_number,order_dow,order_hour_of_day,days_since_prior_order
2539329,1,prior,1,2,08,
2398795,1,prior,2,3,07,15.0
473747,1,prior,3,3,12,21.0

=== order_products__prior.csv ===
order_id,product_id,add_to_cart_order,reordered
2,33120,1,1
2,28985,2,1
2,9327,3,0

=== products.csv ===
product_id,product_name,aisle_id,department_id
1,Chocolate Sandwich Cookies,61,19
2,All-Seasons Salt,104,13
3,Robust Golden Unsweetened Oolong Tea,94,7

=== aisles.csv ===
aisle_id,aisle
1,prepared soups salads
2,specialty cheeses
3,energy granola bars

=== departments.csv ===
department_id,department
1,frozen
2,other
3,bakery
```

The current `notebook.ipynb` only uses `order_products__prior.csv`, `products.csv`, and `departments.csv` (joined on `product_id` and `department_id`) — its `order_products.head()` output already shows the merged result with `order_id, product_id, department_id`.
what is  order_products__prior. is this used anyhow?

`order_products__prior.csv` is the transaction-level table: one row per product in a customer's *prior* (historical, non-training) orders, with columns `order_id, product_id, add_to_cart_order, reordered`.

It's the core dataset the notebook analysis is built on — see cell `619d2766`:

```python
order_products = pd.read_csv(
    f"{DATA_DIR}/order_products__prior.csv",
    usecols=["order_id", "product_id"],
)
```

It loads only `order_id` and `product_id` from it, then merges in each product's `department_id` from `products.csv`. Everything downstream — finding Produce orders, counting co-orders, the ranking and chart — operates on that merged `order_products` table, so `order_products__prior.csv` is effectively the source of every order/product pair used in the whole notebook. `order_products__train.csv` (the other order-products file) isn't touched at all.
what is order_id

`order_id` is the identifier for a single customer order/basket — every row in `order_products__prior.csv` (and `order_products__train.csv`) with the same `order_id` is a product that was purchased together in that one order.

It's also the join key to `orders.csv`, where each `order_id` has exactly one row giving that order's metadata: `user_id` (whose order it was), `eval_set`, `order_number` (that user's Nth order), `order_dow`, `order_hour_of_day`, and `days_since_prior_order`.

In this notebook, `order_id` is used to group product purchases into baskets — e.g. `produce_orders` in cell `df967eae` is the set of distinct `order_id`s that contain at least one Produce item, and `produce_items` filters all rows sharing those same `order_id`s to find what else was bought alongside Produce.
how is correder_counts calculated?

`coorder_counts` (cell `c1145007`) is calculated in two steps:

1. **Filter to Produce-order line items, excluding Produce itself:**
```python
produce_items = order_products[
    order_products["order_id"].isin(produce_orders)
    & order_products["department_id"].ne(produce_id)
]
```
This keeps every product row (`order_id, product_id, department_id`) that belongs to an order in `produce_orders`, but drops the Produce items themselves — so it's "everything else bought alongside Produce."

2. **Count by department:**
```python
coorder_counts = (
    produce_items["department_id"]
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("department_id")
    .reset_index(name="coorder_counts")
    .merge(departments, on="department_id", how="left")
    [["department", "coorder_counts"]]
)
```
`value_counts()` tallies how many `produce_items` rows fall into each `department_id` — i.e., the total number of *individual product purchases* (not distinct orders) from that department that occurred within a Produce order. That count is then labeled with the human-readable `department` name via a merge with `departments.csv`.

So `coorder_counts` = number of line items from each department found in orders that also contained Produce. It's a raw purchase-count, not a per-order or per-customer rate — a single order with 5 dairy items contributes 5 to dairy's count, and departments with more total products/purchases will naturally rank higher regardless of how many distinct orders they appear in.
what is Produce

"Produce" here is one of the 21 department categories in `departments.csv` — the fresh fruits/vegetables department (in the Instacart dataset, `department_id` 4 is `"produce"`).

In cell `df967eae`, the notebook looks it up by name rather than hardcoding the ID:
```python
produce_id = departments.loc[
    departments["department"].eq("produce"),
    "department_id",
].iloc[0]
```
